editorial.headline: Graphic Design’s National Opening—and Bali’s Closed PMA Door
editorial.standfirst: Graphic and visual communication design is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but a foreigner cannot register it through a PMA company in Bali today.
editorial.body:
At its core, this is the professional work of giving information, identity and persuasion a visual form. It encompasses visual-communication and graphic-design services performed manually or digitally; in static, moving or interactive formats; and across printed, screen-based, offline, online and virtual media. The work can appear on phones, television, computers and LED displays as readily as on print. Its subject matter is equally recognisable: brand identities, logos, advertising designs, infographics and stationery all sit within the activity’s stated terrain.

That terrain extends beyond a single logo or campaign. The scope includes communications materials such as posters, brochures, books and other printed matter, together with work for profiles, websites, applications, social media, reports, presentations and promotional materials. It also reaches packaging design—particularly the surface of a package—and environmental graphic design for exhibitions and events, product displays, billboards, wayfinding, signage and building or retail markers. Brand-identity work is expressly part of the picture, from research and brand strategy to the visual identity, logo-use standards, lettering, typeface design and illustration that make a system coherent.

Who may operate in this field is broad in scale: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises. At the national level, the PMA status is TERBUKA and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In practical terms, the national record does not set a foreign-share cap below full ownership for this activity. It is a broad professional-design category, spanning the strategic foundations of a visual identity and the applied materials through which that identity is seen.

Bali is the decisive exception. A foreigner cannot register this activity through a PMA company in Bali today. The block comes from Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium on PMA registration for all Low and Medium-Low risk activities. For this activity, the cited OSS risk at the Besar scale is Low or Medium-Low across every scope, triggering that moratorium. The provincial reason is therefore not a reduced Bali ownership percentage: it is a registration block. National openness does not create a Bali registration pathway for a PMA company under this activity today.
